text:
Sampled ranking can distort model comparisons; a strong margin against one random negative does not establish top-10 discrimination. A [2024 sequential recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compared six negative-sampling strategies across three datasets with 20 repeats: random sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling sometimes balanced head/mid/tail performance at an aggregate accuracy cost. [Rank-estimation research (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/improved-estimation-of-ranks-for-learning-item-recommenders-with-negative-sampling/) demonstrates benefits from correcting sampling-induced rank bias. A [RecSys 2025 evaluation study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines sampler reliability using Kendall’s τ between model rankings, distinguishing sampled-evaluation consistency from recovery of rankings under fully observed preferences.

Practical audit inferred from these findings: define popularity bands using training interaction counts; reuse fixed, unique unseen-item candidate sets containing uniform, popularity-weighted, and popularity-matched negatives. Report positive rank, HR@10, fraction of negatives outranking the positive, and score gaps by target popularity band. Compare against a training-popularity baseline; success limited to uniform negatives or head targets suggests easy-negative success or popularity dependence. Measure checkpoint-order stability across candidate samplers and seeds using Kendall’s τ, then assess whether probe changes track authorized host validation HR@10 within each of the four categories and in their macro-average. These relationships require measurement; the papers do not validate this specific benchmark. Keep exploratory full-catalog ranks and unseen-item recommendation concentration separate from pinned host HR@10, preserving the host’s 200 users/category, 99 negatives, and evaluation seed.
